title: With Due Respect (Vol. 4) -- Ch. 3: Hail to the Court; A Toast to Truth
keywords: Hail to the Court; A Toast to Truth

primary_topics: Chapter 3 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4) -- CJP's February 17, 2008 Inquirer column hailing 'the Puno court for championing press freedom' by stopping the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) from canceling the licenses of stations that aired the 'Hello Garci tapes'

How the decision (written by Chief Justice Puno) condemned the NTC threat as 'an unconstitutional prior restraint... a patent invasion of a constitutionally protected right,' reaffirming a century of jurisprudence that 'content-based' speech restrictions fail unless they meet the 'clear and present danger rule'

CJP's gloss that 'the duty of the judiciary is not to soothe private discomfort but to uphold the Bill of Rights,' and his praise of the ruling and its concurring opinions (Sandoval-Gutierrez's invocation of the Universal Declaration; Carpio's denial of any NTC 'content-based censorship power')

The cautionary 'moral lesson' he draws -- that media must avoid agreeing to 'constitutionally infirm' guidelines or joint statements that can become 'legal traps,' since 'the parameters are already set by the Constitution'
sub_topics: The ruling celebrated: the Supreme Court stopped the NTC from canceling the operating licenses of radio and television stations that aired the so-called 'Hello Garci tapes,' again proving itself 'the bastion of liberty'

The Court's language: written by Chief Justice Reynato Puno, the decision branded the NTC threat 'an unconstitutional prior restraint... a naked means to prevent the free exercise of speech... a patent invasion of a constitutionally protected right,' capped by vintage Puno: 'A blow too soon struck for freedom is preferred than a blow too late'

The doctrine reaffirmed: a century of jurisprudence holds that 'content-based' restrictions on speech cannot stand except under the 'clear and present danger rule' -- which the NTC 'miserably failed to prove'

National security vs. private comfort: airing the conversation 'allegedly between the President... and a high-ranking [Comelec] official' does not endanger national security, though it may cause 'adverse effect on a person's private comfort'

CJP's gloss: 'the duty of the judiciary is not to soothe private discomfort but to uphold the Bill of Rights' -- for had the NTC been allowed to cancel licenses, 'no self-respecting and independent broadcast station would be spared,' leaving the people 'to the mercies of media outlets spouting only government propaganda'

The opinions worth reading: the decision is 'compulsory reading' for its 'scholarly dissertation on media freedom,' with concurrences by Justice Sandoval-Gutierrez (invoking the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and Canadian Chief Justice Beverley McLachlin, whom CJP had invited to the country) and Justice Carpio (that the NTC has no 'content-based censorship power')

The cautionary subtext: separate and dissenting opinions (Justices Chico-Nazario, Velasco, Tinga and Nachura) noted that only a private citizen -- Francisco Chavez, not a media personality -- complained, and that the broadcasters' association (KBP) had issued a 'Joint Press Statement' that the 'NTC respects and will not hinder freedom of the press'

The moral lesson: media 'must be more careful' about agreeing to 'constitutionally infirm "guidelines, standards, parameters, or joint statements"' that could become 'legal traps' for the government to exploit, since 'the parameters are already set by the Constitution. There is no need for any other "guidelines"'

stances.claim: The Court was right to strike the NTC threat as 'an unconstitutional prior restraint': 'content-based' restrictions on speech cannot stand unless they meet the 'clear and present danger rule,' which the NTC 'miserably failed to prove,' since airing the tapes endangered no national security.

notable_anecdotes: 'A blow too soon...': CJP savors Chief Justice Puno's line that 'a blow too soon struck for freedom is preferred than a blow too late' as 'vintage Puno prose.'
The invited Canadian: he notes Justice Sandoval-Gutierrez's citation of Canadian Chief Justice Beverley McLachlin, 'whom I invited to our country when I was Chief Justice.'
A private citizen, not the press: he highlights the dissenters' point that only Francisco Chavez -- a private citizen, not a media personality -- complained of the NTC threat.

The KBP's own words: he flags that the broadcasters' association had issued a 'Joint Press Statement' saying the NTC 'respects and will not hinder freedom of the press' -- the very kind of statement he warns can become a trap.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 3 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 4), CJP's February 17, 2008 Inquirer column, hails 'the Puno court for championing press freedom' after it stopped the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) from canceling the licenses of radio and television stations that aired the 'Hello Garci tapes' -- once more proving the Court 'the bastion of liberty.' Written by Chief Justice Puno, the decision branded the NTC threat 'an unconstitutional prior restraint... a naked means to prevent the free exercise of speech... a patent invasion of a constitutionally protected right,' capped by the line that 'a blow too soon struck for freedom is preferred than a blow too late.' Reaffirming a century of jurisprudence, the Court held that 'content-based' restrictions on speech cannot stand except under the 'clear and present danger rule,' which the NTC 'miserably failed to prove' -- airing the conversation 'allegedly between the President... and a high-ranking [Comelec] official' endangered no national security, even if it caused 'adverse effect on a person's private comfort.' CJP adds that 'the duty of the judiciary is not to soothe private discomfort but to uphold the Bill of Rights,' warning that had the NTC prevailed, 'no self-respecting and independent broadcast station would be spared' and the people would be left to 'government propaganda.' He commends the ruling as 'compulsory reading' for its 'scholarly dissertation on media freedom,' praising Justice Sandoval-Gutierrez's invocation of the Universal Declaration and of Canadian Chief Justice Beverley McLachlin (whom he had invited to the country), and Justice Carpio's view that the NTC has no 'content-based censorship power.' He notes the dissenters' observation that only a private citizen, Francisco Chavez, complained, and that the broadcasters' association (KBP) had itself stated that the 'NTC respects and will not hinder freedom of the press.' His moral lesson: media 'must be more careful' about agreeing to 'constitutionally infirm "guidelines... or joint statements"' that can become 'legal traps,' for 'the parameters are already set by the Constitution. There is no need for any other "guidelines."'
